title: "Everyone felt like we were supporting and building together": An Interview, Part 2
author: Lance Eaton
summary: In the second part of an interview series, a faculty developer who ran a two-year, cross-institutional AI community of practice describes the specific practices that kept the group from decaying into either shallow tool-demo sessions or unproductive ideological debate. She describes a deliberate early rule requiring every session to include someone sharing something that didn't work, a failed prompt or flopped assignment redesign, specifically to counter groups' default gravity toward performative tool demos. She recounts a near-collapse roughly eight months in when a few loud voices turned sessions into AI-maximalist-versus-skeptic debates and quieter members disengaged, and describes how she fixed it not through a rule change but through individual outreach emails asking six people what was actually going on for them, revealing private struggles like grading overload and unprocessed anger about student cheating that had nothing to do with the public debate. Her closing advice to anyone starting a similar group is to resist imposing an agenda or structure early and instead build enough trust that people say the true, unglamorous version of their classroom reality rather than a performed version, which she frames as the entire difference between a group that feels supportive versus one that feels like training or evaluation.
points: Describes a deliberate early rule -- every session must include someone sharing a failed prompt or flopped redesign -- specifically to counter the default gravity of AI communities of practice toward performative tool-demo sessions.
Recounts a near-collapse roughly eight months in when a few loud voices turned sessions into AI-maximalist-versus-skeptic debate and quieter members silently disengaged.

Shows the fix was not a rule change but individual outreach: emailing six disengaged members one-on-one revealed private struggles (grading overload, unprocessed anger about student cheating) invisible in the group's public debate.

Frames the group's core value as the distinction between feeling supported and building together versus feeling trained or evaluated, achieved by resisting agenda and structure in favor of earned trust.
quotes: We never let it become a place where people demoed their AI tool of the week and everyone clapped. That's the default gravity of these groups, and if you don't fight it deliberately, that's what you get.
Every session had to include at least one person saying something that didn't work, a failed prompt, a bad outcome with students, an assignment redesign that flopped.

There was a period, maybe eight months in, where a couple of the loudest voices in the room started treating it like a debate club, arguing AI-maximalist versus AI-skeptic positions at each other, and everyone else just went quiet.
I emailed six people who'd gone quiet and just asked, one on one, what's actually going on for you right now with this. Their answers had almost nothing to do with the debate happening in the group.

The actual value, especially early, is just building enough trust that people will say the true, unglamorous version of what's happening in their classroom instead of the version they think they're supposed to say.
Everyone felt like we were supporting and building together, not like we were being trained or evaluated. That distinction is basically the whole thing.
